entries.eb80875f850bbb3ca5aa2558629fd9b6f0e4c300: <div sID="gen31814" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Eph.2" sID="Eph.2"/> <div eID="gen31814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31815" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31816" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains an account, I. Of the miserable condition of these Ephesians by nature (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.1-Eph.2.3">ver. 1-3</reference>) and again, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.11-Eph.2.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. II. Of the glorious change that was wrought in them by converting grace (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.4-Eph.2.10">ver. 4-10</reference>) and again, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.13">ver. 13</reference>. III. Of the great and mighty privileges that both converted Jews and Gentiles receive from Christ, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14-Eph.2.22">ver. 14-22</reference>. The apostle endeavours to affect them with a due sense of the wonderful change which divine grace had wrought in them; and this is very applicable to that great change which the same grace works in all those who are brought into a state of grace. So that we have here a lively picture both of the misery of unregenerate men and of the happy condition of converted souls, enough to awaken and alarm those who are yet in their sins and to put them upon hastening out of that state, and to comfort and delight those whom God hath quickened, with a consideration of the mighty privileges with which they are invested.
entries.26100ce5f5eed6a1da86f17d81f54928739cbaeb: <div eID="gen31816" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31815" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">State of the Ephesians by Nature. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen31817" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And you <hi type="italic">hath he quickened,</hi> who were dead in trespasses and sins; <hi type="super">2</hi> Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience: <hi type="super">3</hi> Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others. <div eID="gen31817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31818" type="x-p"/> The miserable condition of the Ephesians by nature is here in part described. Observed, 1. Unregenerate souls are dead in trespasses and sins. All those who are in their sins, are dead in sins; yea, in trespasses and sins, which may signify all sorts of sins, habitual and actual, sins of heart and of life. Sin is the death of the soul. Wherever that prevails there is a privation of all spiritual life. Sinners are dead in state, being destitute of the principles, and powers of spiritual life; and cut off from God, the fountain of life: and they are dead in law, as a condemned malefactor is said to be a dead man. 2. A state of sin is a state of conformity to this world, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">v. 2</reference>. In the <reference osisRef="Eph.2.1">first verse</reference> he speaks of their internal state, in this of their outward conversation: <hi type="italic">Wherein,</hi> in which trespasses and sins, <hi type="italic">in time past you walked,</hi> you lived and behaved yourselves in such a manner as the men of the world are used to do. 3. We are by nature bond-slaves to sin and Satan. Those who walk in trespasses and sins, and according to the course of this world, walk <hi type="italic">according to the prince of the power of the air.</hi> The devil, or the prince of devils, is thus described. See <reference osisRef="Matt.12.24">Matt. xii. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.26">26</reference>. The legions of apostate angels are as one power united under one chief; and therefore what is called <hi type="italic">the powers of darkness</hi> elsewhere is here spoken of in the singular number. The air is represented as the seat of his kingdom: and it was the opinion of both Jews and heathens that the air is full of spirits, and that there they exercise and exert themselves. The devil seems to have some power (by God's permission) in the lower region of the air; there he is at hand to tempt men, and to do as much mischief to the world as he can: but it is the comfort and joy of God's people that he who is <hi type="italic">head over all things to the church</hi> has conquered the devil and has him in his chain. But wicked men are slaves to Satan, for they walk according to him; they conform their lives and actions to the will and pleasure of this great usurper. The course and tenour of their lives are according to his suggestions, and in compliance with his temptations; they are subject to him, and are led captive by him at his will, whereupon he is called the god of this world, and <hi type="italic">the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience. The children of disobedience</hi> are such as choose to disobey God, and to serve the devil; in these he works very powerfully and effectually. As the good Spirit works that which is good in obedient souls, so this evil spirit works that which is evil in wicked men; and he now works, not only heretofore, but even since the world has been blessed with the light of the glorious gospel. The apostle adds, <hi type="italic">Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past,</hi> which words refer to the Jews, whom he signifies here to have been in the like sad and miserable condition by nature, and to have been as vile and wicked as the unregenerate Gentiles themselves, and whose natural state he further describes in the next words. 4. We are by nature drudges to the flesh, and to our corrupt affections, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.3">v. 3</reference>. By <hi type="italic">fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind,</hi> men contract that filthiness of flesh and spirit from which the apostle exhorts Christians to cleanse themselves, <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.1">2 Cor. vii. 1</reference>. The fulfilling of the desires of the flesh and of the mind includes all the sin and wickedness that are acted in and by both the inferior and the higher or nobler powers of the soul. We lived in the actual commission of all those sins to which corrupt nature inclined us. The carnal mind makes a man a perfect slave to his vicious appetite.—<hi type="italic">The fulfilling of the wills of the flesh,</hi> so the words may be rendered, denoting the efficacy of these lusts, and what power they have over those who yield themselves up unto them. 5. We are <hi type="italic">by nature the children of wrath, even as others.</hi> The Jews were so, as well as the Gentiles; and one man is as much so as another by nature, not only by custom and imitation, but from the time when we began to exist, and by reason of our natural inclinations and appetites. All men, being naturally children of disobedience, are also by nature children of wrath: God is angry with the wicked every day. Our state and course are such as deserve wrath, and would end in eternal wrath, if divine grace did not interpose. What reason have sinners then to be looking out for that grace that will make them, of children of wrath, children of God and heirs of glory! Thus far the apostle has described the misery of a natural state in <reference osisRef="Eph.2.1-Eph.2.3">these verses</reference>, which we shall find him pursuing again in some following ones.
entries.fc1a72484d79498c7768234fb66b34fdc56f4f0e: <div eID="gen31818" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Change Wrought in the Ephesians. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen31819" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, <hi type="super">5</hi> Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;) <hi type="super">6</hi> And hath raised <hi type="italic">us</hi> up together, and made <hi type="italic">us</hi> sit together in heavenly <hi type="italic">places</hi> in Christ Jesus: 7 That in the ages to come he might show the exceeding riches of his grace in <hi type="italic">his</hi> kindness toward us through Christ Jesus. <hi type="super">8</hi> For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: <hi type="italic">it is</hi> the gift of God: <hi type="super">9</hi> Not of works, lest any man should boast. <hi type="super">10</hi> For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them. <div eID="gen31819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31820" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle begins his account of the glorious change that was wrought in them by converting grace, where observe, <div eID="gen31820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31821" type="x-p"/> I. By whom, and in what manner, it was brought about and effected. 1. Negatively: <hi type="italic">Not of yourselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.8">v. 8</reference>. Our faith, our conversion, and our eternal salvation, are not the mere product of any natural abilities, nor of any merit of our own: <hi type="italic">Not of works, lest any man should boast,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.9">v. 9</reference>. These things are not brought to pass by any thing done by us, and therefore all boasting is excluded; he who glories must not glory in himself, but in the Lord. There is no room for any man's boasting of his own abilities and power; or as though he had done any thing that might deserve such immense favours from God. 2. Positively: <hi type="italic">But God, who is rich in mercy,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Eph.2.4">v. 4</reference>. God himself is the author of this great and happy change, and his great love is the spring and fontal cause of it; hence he resolved to show mercy. Love is his inclination to do us good considered simply as creatures; mercy respects us as apostate and as miserable creatures. Observe, God's eternal love or good-will towards his creatures is the fountain whence all his mercies vouch-safed to us proceed; and that love of God is great love, and that mercy of his is rich mercy, inexpressibly great and inexhaustibly rich. And then <hi type="italic">by grace you are saved</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.5">v. 5</reference>), and <hi type="italic">by grace are you saved through faith—it is the gift of</hi> God, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.8">v. 8</reference>. Note, Every converted sinner is a saved sinner. Such are delivered from sin and wrath; they are brought into a state of salvation, and have a right given them by grace to eternal happiness. The grace that saves them is the free undeserved goodness and favour of God; and he saves them, not <hi type="italic">by the works of the law,</hi> but through faith in Christ Jesus, by means of which they come to partake of the great blessings of the gospel; and both that faith and that salvation on which it has so great an influence are the gift of God. The great objects of faith are made known by divine revelation, and made credible by the testimony and evidence which God hath given us; and that we believe to salvation and obtain salvation through faith is entirely owing to divine assistance and grace; God has ordered all so that the whole shall appear to be of grace. Observe, <div eID="gen31821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31822" type="x-p"/> II. Wherein this change consists, in several particulars, answering to the misery of our natural state, some of which are enumerated in this section, and others are mentioned below. 1. We who were dead are quickened (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.5">v. 5</reference>), we are saved from the death of sin and have a principle of spiritual life implanted in us. Grace in the soul is a new life in the soul. As death locks up the senses, seals up all the powers and faculties, so does a state of sin, as to any thing that is good. Grace unlocks and opens all, and enlarges the soul. Observe, A regenerate sinner becomes a living soul: he lives a life of sanctification, being born of God; and he lives in the sense of the law, being delivered from the guilt of sin by pardoning and justifying grace. <hi type="italic">He hath quickened us together with Christ.</hi> Our spiritual life results from our union with Christ; it is in him that we live: <hi type="italic">Because I live, you shall live also.</hi> 2. We who were buried are raised up, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.6">v. 6</reference>. What remains yet to be done is here spoken of as though it were already past, though indeed we are raised up in virtue of our union with him whom God hath raised from the dead. When he raised Christ from the dead, he did in effect raise up all believers together with him, he being their common head; and when he placed him at his right hand in heavenly places, he advanced and glorified them in and with him, their raised and exalted head and forerunner.—<hi type="italic">And made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus.</hi> This may be understood in another sense. Sinners roll themselves in the dust; sanctified souls sit in heavenly places, are raised above the world; the world is as nothing to them, compared with what it has been, and compared with what the other world is. Saints are not only Christ's freemen, but they are assessors with him; by the assistance of his grace they have ascended with him above this world to converse with another, and they live in the constant expectation of it. They are not only servants to the best of masters in the best work, but they are exalted to reign with him; they sit upon the throne with Christ, <hi type="italic">as he has sat down with his Father on his throne.</hi> <div eID="gen31822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31823" type="x-p"/> III. Observe what is the great design and aim of God in producing and effecting this change: And this, 1. With respect to others: <hi type="italic">That in the ages to come he might show,</hi> &c. (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.7">v. 7</reference>), that he might give a specimen and proof of his great goodness and mercy, for the encouragement of sinners in future time. Observe, The goodness of God in converting and saving sinners heretofore is a proper encouragement to others in after-time to hope in his grace and mercy, and to apply themselves to these. God having this in his design, poor sinners should take great encouragement from it. And what may we not hope for from such grace and kindness, from riches of grace, to which this change is owing? <hi type="italic">Through Christ Jesus,</hi> by and through whom God conveys all his favour and blessings to us. 2. With respect to the regenerated sinners themselves: <hi type="italic">For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Eph.2.10">v. 10</reference>. It appears that all is of grace, because all our spiritual advantages are from God. <hi type="italic">We are his workmanship;</hi> he means in respect of the new creation; not only as men, but as saints. The new man is a new creature; and God is its Creator. It is a new birth, and we are born or begotten of his will. <hi type="italic">In Christ Jesus,</hi> that is, on the account of what he has done and suffered, and by the influence and operation of his blessed Spirit. <hi type="italic">Unto good works,</hi> &c. The apostle having before ascribed this change to divine grace in exclusion of works, lest he should seem thereby to discourage good works, he here observes that though the change is to be ascribed to nothing of that nature (<hi type="italic">for we are the workmanship of God</hi>), yet God, in his new creation, has designed and prepared us for good works: <hi type="italic">Created unto good works,</hi> with a design that we should be fruitful in them. Wherever God by his grace implants good principles, they are intended to be for good works. <hi type="italic">Which God hath before ordained,</hi> that is, decreed and appointed. Or, the words may be read, <hi type="italic">To which God hath before prepared us,</hi> that is, by blessing us with the knowledge of his will, and with the assistance of his Holy Spirit; and by producing such a change in us. <hi type="italic">That we should walk in them,</hi> or glorify God by an exemplary conversation and by our perseverance in holiness.
entries.9a1c5a9b62c7c801917576af64432a02f48f91f5: <div eID="gen31823" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Miserable Condition of the Ephesians by Nature. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen31824" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Wherefore remember, that ye <hi type="italic">being</hi> in time past Gentiles in the flesh, who are called Uncircumcision by that which is called the Circumcision in the flesh made by hands; 12 That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world: <hi type="super">13</hi> But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ. <div eID="gen31824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31825" type="x-p"/> In these verses the apostle proceeds in his account of the miserable condition of these Ephesians by nature. <hi type="italic">Wherefore remember,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Eph.2.11">v. 11</reference>. As if he had said, "You should remember what you have been, and compare it with what you now are, in order to humble yourselves and to excite your love and thankfulness to God." Note, Converted sinners ought frequently to reflect upon the sinfulness and misery of the state they were in by nature. <hi type="italic">Gentiles in the flesh,</hi> that is, living in the corruption of their natures, and being destitute of circumcision, the outward sign of an interest in the covenant of grace. <hi type="italic">Who are called uncircumcision by that,</hi> &c., that is, "You were reproached and upbraided for it by the formal Jews, who made an external profession, and who looked no further than the outward ordinance." Note, Hypocritical professors are wont to value themselves chiefly on their external privileges, and to reproach and despise others who are destitute of them. The apostle describes the misery of their case in several particulars, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.12">v. 12</reference>. "<hi type="italic">At that time,</hi> while you were Gentiles, and in an unconverted state, you were," 1. "In a Christless condition, without the knowledge of the Messiah, and without any saving interest in him or relation to him." It is true of all unconverted sinners, all those who are destitute of faith, that they have no saving interest in Christ; and it must be a sad and deplorable thing for a soul to be without a Christ. Being without Christ, they were, 2. <hi type="italic">Aliens from the commonwealth of Israel;</hi> they did not belong to Christ's church, and had no communion with it, that being confined to the Israelitish nation. It is no small privilege to be placed in the church of Christ, and to share with the members of it in the advantages peculiar to it. 3. <hi type="italic">They are strangers from the covenants of promise.</hi> The covenant of grace has ever been the same for substance, though, having undergone various additions and improvements in the several ages of the church, it is called covenants; and the covenants of promise, because it is made up of promises, and particularly contains the great promise of the Messiah, and of eternal life through him. Now the Ephesians, in their gentilism, were strangers to this covenant, having never had any information nor overture of it; and all unregenerate sinners are strangers to it, as they have no interest in it. Those who are without Christ, and so have no interest in the Mediator of the covenant, have none in the promises of the covenant. 4. They had no hope, that is, beyond this life—no well-grounded hope in God, no hope of spiritual and eternal blessings. Those who are with out Christ, and strangers from the covenant, can have no good hope; for Christ and the covenant are the ground and foundation of all the Christian's hopes. They were in a state of distance and estrangement from God: <hi type="italic">Without God in the world;</hi> not without some general knowledge of a deity, for they worshipped idols, but living without any due regard to him, any acknowledged dependence on him, and any special interest in him. The words are, <hi type="italic">atheists in the world;</hi> for, though they worshipped many gods, yet they were without the true God. <div eID="gen31825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31826" type="x-p"/> The apostle proceeds (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.13">v. 13</reference>) further to illustrate the happy change that was made in their state: <hi type="italic">But now, in Christ Jesus, you who sometimes were far off,</hi> &c. They were far off from Christ, from his church, from the promises, from the Christian hope, and from God himself; and therefore from all good, like the prodigal son in the far country: this had been represented in the <reference osisRef="Eph.2.11-Eph.2.13">preceding verses</reference>. Unconverted sinners remove themselves at a distance from God, and God puts them at a distance: <hi type="italic">He be holds the proud afar off. "But now in Christ Jesus,</hi> &c., upon your conversion, by virtue of union with Christ, and interest in him by faith, you are made nigh." They were brought home to God, received into the church, taken into the covenant, and possessed of all other privileges consequent upon these. Note, <hi type="italic">The saints are a people near to God. Salvation is far from the wicked;</hi> but God is a help at hand to his people; and this is <hi type="italic">by the blood of Christ,</hi> by the merit of his sufferings and death. Every believing sinner owes his nearness to God, and his interest in his favour, to the death and sacrifice of Christ.
entries.eaced00243fb558b2c213394558fd4de57a952fb: <div eID="gen31826" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Union of Jews and Gentiles. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen31827" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition <hi type="italic">between us;</hi> <hi type="super">15</hi> Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the law of commandments <hi type="italic">contained</hi> in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, <hi type="italic">so</hi> making peace; <hi type="super">16</hi> And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby: <hi type="super">17</hi> And came and preached peace to you which were afar off, and to them that were nigh. <hi type="super">18</hi> For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father. <hi type="super">19</hi> Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God; <hi type="super">20</hi> And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner <hi type="italic">stone;</hi> <hi type="super">21</hi> In whom all the building fitly framed together groweth unto a holy temple in the Lord: 22 In whom ye also are builded together for a habitation of God through the Spirit. <div eID="gen31827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31828" type="x-p"/> We have now come to the last part of the chapter, which contains an account of the great and mighty privileges that converted Jews and Gentiles both receive from Christ. The apostle here shows that those who were in a state of enmity are reconciled. Between the Jews and the Gentiles there had been a great enmity; so there is between God and every unregenerate man. Now Jesus Christ is our peace, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">v. 14</reference>. He made peace by the sacrifice of himself; and came to reconcile, 1. Jews and Gentiles to each other. He <hi type="italic">made both one,</hi> by reconciling these two divisions of men, who were wont to malign, to hate, and to reproach each other before. He <hi type="italic">broke down the middle wall of partition,</hi> the ceremonial law, that made the great feud, and was the badge of the Jews' peculiarity, called <hi type="italic">the partition-wall</hi> by way of allusion to the partition in the temple, which separated the court of the Gentiles from that into which the Jews only had liberty to enter. Thus <hi type="italic">he abolished in his flesh the enmity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.15">v. 15</reference>. By his sufferings in the flesh, to took away the binding power of the ceremonial law (so removing that cause of enmity and distance between them), which is here called <hi type="italic">the law of commandments contained in ordinances,</hi> because it enjoined a multitude of external rites and ceremonies, and consisted of many institutions and appointments about the outward parts of divine worship. <hi type="italic">The legal ceremonies were abrogated by Christ, having their accomplishment in him.</hi> By taking these out of the way, he formed one church of believers, whether they had been Jews or Gentiles. Thus he made <hi type="italic">in himself of twain one new man.</hi> He framed both these parties into one new society, or body of God's people, uniting them to himself as their common head, they being renewed by the Holy Ghost, and now concurring in a new way of gospel worship, <hi type="italic">so making peace</hi> between these two parties, who were so much at variance before. 2. There is an enmity between God and sinners, whether Jews and Gentiles; and Christ came to slay that enmity, and to reconcile them both to God, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.16">v. 16</reference>. Sin breeds a quarrel between God and men. Christ came to take up the quarrel, and to bring it to an end, by reconciling both Jew and Gentile, now collected and gathered into one body, to a provoked and an offended God: and this <hi type="italic">by the cross,</hi> or by the sacrifice of himself upon the cross, <hi type="italic">having slain the enmity thereby.</hi> He, being slain or sacrificed, slew the enmity that there was between God and poor sinners. The apostle proceeds to illustrate the great advantages which both parties gain by the mediation of our Lord Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.17">v. 17</reference>. Christ, who purchased peace on the cross, came, partly in his own person, as to the Jews, who are here said to have been nigh, and partly in his apostles, whom he commissioned to preach the gospel to the Gentiles, who are said to have been afar off, in the sense that has been given before. <hi type="italic">And preached peace,</hi> or published the terms of reconciliation with God and of eternal life. Note here, When the messengers of Christ deliver his truths, it is in effect the same as if he did it immediately himself. He is said to preach by them, insomuch that he who receiveth them receiveth him, and he who despiseth them (acting by virtue of his commission, and delivering his message) despiseth and rejecteth Christ himself. Now the effect of this peace is the free access which both Jews and Gentiles have unto God (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">For through him,</hi> in his name and by virtue of his mediation, <hi type="italic">we both have access</hi> or admission into the presence of God, who has become the common reconciled Father of both: the throne of grace is erected for us to come to, and liberty of approach to that throne is allowed us. Our access is by the Holy Spirit. Christ purchased for us leave to come to God, and the Spirit gives us a heart to come and strength to come, even grace to serve God acceptably. Observe, We draw nigh to God, through Jesus Christ, by the help of the Spirit. The Ephesians, upon their conversion, having such an access to God, as well as the Jews, and by the same Spirit, the apostle tells them, <hi type="italic">Now therefore you are no more strangers and foreigners,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.19">v. 19</reference>. This he mentions by way of opposition to what he had observed of them in their heathenism: they were now no longer <hi type="italic">aliens from the commonwealth of Israel,</hi> and no longer what the Jews were wont to account all the nations of the earth besides themselves (namely, strangers to God), <hi type="italic">but fellow-citizens with the saints, and of the household of God,</hi> that is, members of the church of Christ, and having a right to all the privileges of it. Observe here, The church is compared to a city, and every converted sinner is free of it. It is also compared to a house, and every converted sinner is one of the domestics, one of the family, a servant and a child in God's house. In <reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">v. 20</reference> the church is compared to a building. The apostles and prophets are <hi type="italic">the foundation</hi> of that building. They may be so called in a secondary sense, Christ himself being the primary foundation; but we are rather to understand it of the doctrine delivered by the prophets of the Old Testament and the apostles of the New. It follows, <hi type="italic">Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner-stone.</hi> In him both Jews and Gentiles meet, and constitute one church; and Christ supports the building by his strength: <hi type="italic">In whom all the building, fitly framed together,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Eph.2.21">v. 21</reference>. All believers, of whom it consists, being united to Christ by faith, and among themselves by Christian charity, <hi type="italic">grow unto a holy temple,</hi> become a sacred society, in which there is much communion between God and his people, as in the temple, they worshipping and serving him, he manifesting himself unto them, they offering up spiritual sacrifices to God and he dispensing his blessings and favours to them. Thus the building, for the nature of it, is a temple, a holy temple; for the church is the place which God hath chosen to put his name there, and it becomes such a temple by grace and strength derived from himself—<hi type="italic">in the Lord.</hi> The universal church being built upon Christ as the foundation-stone, and united in Christ as the corner-stone, comes at length to be glorified in him as the top-stone: <hi type="italic">In whom you also are built together,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Eph.2.22">v. 22</reference>. Observe, Not only the universal church is called the temple of God, but particular churches; and even every true believer is a living temple, is <hi type="italic">a habitation of God through the Spirit.</hi> God dwells in all believers now, they having become the temple of God through the operations of the blessed Spirit, and his dwelling with them now is an earnest of their dwelling together with him to eternity.  <chapter eID="Eph.2"/> <div eID="gen31828" type="x-p"/>

entries.495ec875b60c133f25d6d0d03eef31a14544bcb7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17594"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Eph.2.1-Eph.2.22">Ep 2:1-22</reference>. God's Love and Grace in Quickening Us, Once Dead, through Christ. His Purpose in Doing So: Exhortation Based on Our Privileges as Built Together, an Holy Temple, in Christ, through the Spirit.</title> <div sID="gen35445" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17594"/><hi type="bold">1. And you--</hi>"You also," among those who have experienced His mighty power in enabling them to believe (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.19-Eph.1.23">Ep 1:19-23</reference>).<div eID="gen35445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35446" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath he quickened--</hi>supplied from the Greek (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.5">Ep 2:5</reference>).<div eID="gen35446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35447" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dead--</hi>spiritually. (<reference osisRef="Col.2.13">Col 2:13</reference>). A living corpse: without the gracious presence of God's Spirit in the soul, and so unable to think, will, or do aught that is holy.<div eID="gen35447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in trespasses ... sins--</hi>in them, as the element in which the unbeliever is, and through which he is dead to the true life. Sin is the death of the soul. <reference osisRef="Isa.9.2">Is 9:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.25">Joh 5:25</reference>, "dead" (spiritually), <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.6">1Ti 5:6</reference>. "Alienated from the life of God" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Ep 4:18</reference>). Translate, as Greek, "in your trespasses," &c. "Trespass" in Greek, expresses a FALL or LAPSE, such as the transgression of Adam whereby he fell. "Sin." (Greek, "hamartia") implies innate corruption and ALIENATION from God (literally, erring of the mind from the rule of truth), exhibited in acts of sin (Greek, "hamartemata"). Bengel, refers "trespasses" to the Jews who had the law, and yet revolted from it; "sins," to the Gentiles who know not God. <div eID="gen35448" type="x-p"/>
entries.64df250e0b3ba9f3ae21a66815fca447e9995cf9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17595"/><div sID="gen35449" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17595"/><hi type="bold">2. the course of this world--</hi>the career (literally, "the age," compare <reference osisRef="Gal.1.4">Ga 1:4</reference>), or present system of this world (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6">1Co 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">3:18</reference>, 19, as opposed to "the world to come"): alien from God, and lying in the wicked one (<reference osisRef="1John.5.19">1Jo 5:19</reference>). "The age" (which is something more external and ethical) regulates "the world" (which is something more external).<div eID="gen35449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35450" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the prince of the power of the air--</hi>the unseen God who lies underneath guiding "the course of this world" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2Co 4:4</reference>); ranging through the air around us: compare <reference osisRef="Mark.4.4">Mr 4:4</reference>, "fowls of the air" (Greek, "heaven") that is, (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.15">Ep 2:15</reference>), "Satan" and his demons. Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Ep 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.31">Joh 12:31</reference>. Christ's ascension seems to have cast Satan out of heaven (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.5">Re 12:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.9.10">9, 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.13">12, 13</reference>), where he had been heretofore the accuser of the brethren (<reference osisRef="Job.1.6-Job.1.11">Job 1:6-11</reference>). No longer able to accuse in heaven those justified by Christ, the ascended Saviour (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.33">Ro 8:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.34">34</reference>), he assails them on earth with all trials and temptations; and "we live in an atmosphere poisonous and impregnated with deadly elements. But a mighty purification of the air will be effected by Christ's coming" [Auberlen], for Satan shall be bound (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.12">Re 12:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.15">13, 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.2">20:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.3">3</reference>). "The power" is here used collectively for the "powers of the air"; in apposition with which "powers" stand the "spirits," comprehended in the singular, "the spirit," taken also collectively: the aggregate of the "seducing spirits" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1">1Ti 4:1</reference>) which "work now (still; not merely, as in your case, 'in time past') in the sons of disobedience" (a Hebraism: men who are not merely by accident disobedient, but who are essentially sons of disobedience itself: compare <reference osisRef="Matt.3.7">Mt 3:7</reference>), and of which Satan is here declared to be "the prince." The Greek does not allow "the spirit" to refer to Satan, "the prince" himself, but to "the powers of the air" of which he is prince. The powers of the air are the embodiment of that evil "spirit" which is the ruling principle of unbelievers, especially the heathen (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.18">Ac 26:18</reference>), as opposed to the spirit of the children of God (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.33">Lu 4:33</reference>). The potency of that "spirit" is shown in the "disobedience" of the former. Compare <reference osisRef="Deut.32.20">De 32:20</reference>, "children in whom is no faith" (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.9">Is 30:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.4">57:4</reference>). They disobey the Gospel both in faith and practice (<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.8">2Th 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">2Co 2:12</reference>). <div eID="gen35450" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d67a4ddf3aeba597178d786b7020c923c2d8171: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17596"/><div sID="gen35451" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17596"/><hi type="bold">3. also we--</hi>that is, we also. Paul here joins himself in the same category with them, passing from the second person (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.1">Ep 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.2">2</reference>) to the first person here.<div eID="gen35451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35452" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all--</hi>Jews and Gentiles.<div eID="gen35452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35453" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our conversation--</hi>"our way of life" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">2Co 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.18">1Pe 1:18</reference>). This expression implies an outwardly more decorous course, than the open "walk" in gross sins on the part of the majority of Ephesians in times past, the Gentile portion of whom may be specially referred to in <reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference>. Paul and his Jewish countrymen, though outwardly more seemly than the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.4">Ac 26:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.5.18">5, 18</reference>), had been essentially like them in living to the unrenewed flesh, without the Spirit of God.<div eID="gen35453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35454" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fulfilling--</hi>Greek, doing.<div eID="gen35454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35455" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mind--</hi>Greek, "our thoughts." Mental suggestions and purposes (independent of God), as distinguished from the blind impulses of "the flesh."<div eID="gen35455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35456" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and were by nature--</hi>He intentionally breaks off the construction, substituting "and we were" for "and being," to mark emphatically his and their past state by nature, as contrasted with their present state by grace. Not merely is it, we had our way of life fulfilling our fleshly desires, and so being children of wrath; but we were by nature originally "children of wrath," and so consequently had our way of life fulfilling our fleshly desires. "Nature," in Greek, implies that which has grown in us as the peculiarity of our being, growing with our growth, and strengthening with our strength, as distinguished from that which has been wrought on us by mere external influences: what is inherent, not acquired (<reference osisRef="Job.14.4">Job 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.5">Psa 51:5</reference>). An incidental proof of the doctrine of original sin.<div eID="gen35456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35457" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children of wrath--</hi>not merely "sons," as in the Greek, "sons of disobedience" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference>), but "children" by generation; not merely by adoption, as "sons" might be. The Greek order more emphatically marks this innate corruption: "Those who in their (very) nature are children of wrath"; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.5">Ep 2:5</reference>, "grace" is opposed to "nature" here; and salvation (implied in <reference osisRef="Eph.2.5">Ep 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>, "saved") to "wrath." Compare Article IX, Church of England Common Prayer Book. "Original sin (birth-sin), standeth not in the following of Adam, but is the fault and corruption of the nature of every man, naturally engendered of Adam [Christ was supernaturally conceived by the Holy Ghost of the Virgin], whereby man is very far gone from original righteousness, and is of his own nature inclined to evil; and therefore, in every person born into this world, it deserveth God's wrath and damnation." Paul shows that even the Jews, who boasted of their birth from Abraham, were by natural birth equally children of wrath as the Gentiles, whom the Jews despised on account of their birth from idolaters (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.9">Ro 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.12-Rom.5.14">5:12-14</reference>). "Wrath abideth" on all who disobey the Gospel in faith and practice (<reference osisRef="John.3.36">Joh 3:36</reference>). The phrase, "children of wrath," is a Hebraism, that is, objects of God's wrath from childhood, in our natural state, as being born in the sin which God hates. So "son of death" (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.5">2Sa 12:5</reference>, Margin); "son of perdition" (<reference osisRef="John.17.12">Joh 17:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.3">2Th 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen35457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35458" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as others--</hi>Greek, "as the rest" of mankind are (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13">1Th 4:13</reference>). <div eID="gen35458" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6629d5f75bfaa9f97a72b0119552b9be8fab857: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17597"/><div sID="gen35459" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17597"/><hi type="bold">4. God, who is rich--</hi>Greek "(as) being rich in mercy."<div eID="gen35459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35460" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for--</hi>that is, "because of His great love." This was the special ground of God's saving us; as "rich in mercy" (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.2.7">Ep 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.2.4">Ro 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.12">10:12</reference>) was the general ground. "Mercy takes away misery; love confers salvation" [Bengel]. <div eID="gen35460" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce308170af161a0f0bcb953c72be09608082072f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17598"/><div sID="gen35461" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17598"/><hi type="bold">5. dead in sins--</hi>The best reading is in the Greek, "dead in our (literally, 'the') trespasses."<div eID="gen35461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">quickened--</hi>"vivified" spiritually, and consequences hereafter, corporally. There must be a spiritual resurrection of the soul before there can be a comfortable resurrection of the body [Pearson] (<reference osisRef="John.11.25">Joh 11:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.11.26">26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.11">Ro 8:11</reference>).<div eID="gen35462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35463" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">together with Christ--</hi>The Head being seated at God's right hand, the body also sits there with Him [Chrysostom]. We are already seated there IN Him ("in Christ Jesus," <reference osisRef="Eph.2.6">Ep 2:6</reference>), and hereafter shall be seated by Him; IN Him already as in our Head, which is the ground of our hope; by Him hereafter, as by the conferring cause, when hope shall be swallowed up in fruition [Pearson]. What God wrought in Christ, He wrought (by the very fact) in all united to Christ, and one with Him.<div eID="gen35463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35464" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by grace ye are saved--</hi>Greek, "Ye are in a saved state." Not merely "ye are being saved," but ye "are passed from death unto life" (<reference osisRef="John.5.24">Joh 5:24</reference>). Salvation is to the Christian not a thing to be waited for hereafter, but already realized (<reference osisRef="1John.3.14">1Jo 3:14</reference>). The parenthetic introduction of this clause here (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.2.8">Ep 2:8</reference>) is a burst of Paul's feeling, and in order to make the Ephesians feel that grace from first to last is the sole source of salvation; hence, too, he says "ye," not "we." <div eID="gen35464" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd01d9a49c269abd8d839fe3419500241765d4e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17599"/><div sID="gen35465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17599"/><hi type="bold">6. raised us up together--</hi>with Christ. The "raising up" presupposes previous quickening of Jesus in the tomb, and of us in the grave of our sins.<div eID="gen35465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35466" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made us sit together--</hi>with Christ, namely, in His ascension. Believers are bodily in heaven in point of right, and virtually so in spirit, and have each their own place assigned there, which in due time they shall take possession of (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">21</reference>). He does not say, "on the right hand of God"; a prerogative reserved to Christ peculiarly; though they shall share His throne (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Re 3:21</reference>).<div eID="gen35466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35467" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Christ Jesus--</hi>Our union with Him is the ground of our present spiritual, and future bodily, resurrection and ascension. "Christ Jesus" is the phrase mostly used in this Epistle, in which the office of the Christ, the Anointed Prophet, Priest and King, is the prominent thought; when the Person is prominent, "Jesus Christ" is the phrase used. <div eID="gen35467" type="x-p"/>
entries.f96e9512d9b77604d53ee20b15d36b7c398cd8be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17600"/><div sID="gen35468" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17600"/>7. Greek, "That He might show forth (middle reflexive voice; for His own glory, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Ep 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.14">12, 14</reference>) in the ages which are coming on," that is, the blessed ages of the Gospel which supersede "the age (Greek, for 'course') of this world" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference>), and the past "ages" from which the mystery was hidden (<reference osisRef="Col.1.26">Col 1:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27">27</reference>). These good ages, though beginning with the first preaching of the Gospel, and thenceforth continually succeeding one another, are not consummated till the Lord's coming again (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.1.21">Ep 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.5">He 6:5</reference>). The words, "coming on," do not exclude the time then present, but imply simply the ages following upon Christ's "raising them up together" spiritually (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.6">Ep 2:6</reference>).<div eID="gen35468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35469" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kindness--</hi>"benignity."<div eID="gen35469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35470" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through Christ--</hi>rather, as Greek, "in Christ"; the same expression as is so often repeated, to mark that all our blessings center "IN Him." <div eID="gen35470" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8a142e6e5fdab404e2143720d077ae7f31d16a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17601"/><div sID="gen35471" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17601"/><hi type="bold">8. For--</hi>illustrating "the exceeding riches of His grace in kindness." Translate as in <reference osisRef="Eph.2.5">Ep 2:5</reference>, "Ye are in a saved state."<div eID="gen35471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through faith--</hi>the effect of the power of Christ's resurrection (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">Ep 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.10">Php 3:10</reference>) whereby we are "raised together" with Him (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.6">Ep 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.12">Col 2:12</reference>). Some of the oldest manuscripts read, "through your (literally, 'the') faith." The instrument or mean of salvation on the part of the person saved; Christ alone is the meritorious agent.<div eID="gen35472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35473" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and that--</hi>namely, the act of believing, or "faith." "Of yourselves" stands in opposition to, "it is the gift of God" (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.29">Php 1:29</reference>). "That which I have said, 'through faith,' I do not wish to be understood so as if I excepted faith itself from grace" [Estius]. "God justifies the believing man, not for the worthiness of his belief, but for the worthiness of Him in whom he believes" [Hooker]. The initiation, as well as the increase, of faith, is from the Spirit of God, not only by an external proposal of the word, but by internal illumination in the soul [Pearson]. Yet "faith" cometh by the means which man must avail himself of, namely, "hearing the word of God" (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.17">Ro 10:17</reference>), and prayer (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.13">Lu 11:13</reference>), though the blessing is wholly of God (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.6">1Co 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.7">7</reference>). <div eID="gen35473" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c99c90b48cd034278195deb900f423b7d18039e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17602"/><div sID="gen35474" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17602"/><hi type="bold">9. Not of works--</hi>This clause stands in contrast to "by grace," as is confirmed by <reference osisRef="Rom.4.4">Ro 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.6">11:6</reference>.<div eID="gen35474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35475" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lest--</hi>rather, as Greek, "that no man should boast" (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.27">Ro 3:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.4.2">4:2</reference>). <div eID="gen35475" type="x-p"/>
entries.29aa961dea18ce2169f5fb0cd09e49389be7ca0c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17603"/><div sID="gen35476" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17603"/><hi type="bold">10. workmanship--</hi>literally, "a thing of His making"; "handiwork." Here the spiritual creation, not the physical, is referred to (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.8">Ep 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen35476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35477" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">created--</hi>having been created (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.24">Ep 4:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.18">Psa 102:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.21">Is 43:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.5">2Co 5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.17">17</reference>).<div eID="gen35477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35478" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto good works--</hi>"for good works." "Good works" cannot be performed until we are new "created unto" them. Paul never calls the works of the law "good works." We are not saved by, but created unto, good works.<div eID="gen35478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35479" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before ordained--</hi>Greek, "before made ready" (compare <reference osisRef="John.5.36">Joh 5:36</reference>). God marks out for each in His purposes beforehand, the particular good works, and the time and way which tie sees best. God both makes ready by His providence the opportunities for the works, and makes us ready for their performance (<reference osisRef="John.15.16">Joh 15:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.21">2Ti 2:21</reference>).<div eID="gen35479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35480" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that we should walk in them--</hi>not "be saved" by them. Works do not justify, but the justified man works (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.22-Gal.5.25">Ga 5:22-25</reference>). <div eID="gen35480" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d516a65e30638eca8df6736168c31c7f035eea0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17604"/><div sID="gen35481" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17604"/>11. The Greek order in the oldest manuscripts is, "That in time past (literally, once) ye," &c. Such remembrance sharpens gratitude and strengthens faith (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.19">Ep 2:19</reference>) [Bengel].<div eID="gen35481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35482" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gentiles in the flesh--</hi>that is, Gentiles in respect to circumcision.<div eID="gen35482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35483" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">called Uncircumcision--</hi>The Gentiles were called (in contempt), and were, the Uncircumcision; the Jews were called, but were not truly, the Circumcision [Ellicott].<div eID="gen35483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the flesh made by hands--</hi>as opposed to the true "circumcision of the heart in the Spirit, and not the letter" (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.29">Ro 2:29</reference>), "made without the hands in putting off the body of the sins of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.11">Col 2:11</reference>). <div eID="gen35484" type="x-p"/>
entries.95d51a463f93ddccd6d21e021c35616ff252b2f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17605"/><div sID="gen35485" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17605"/><hi type="bold">12. without Christ--</hi>Greek, "separate from Christ"; having no part in Him; far from Him. A different Greek word (aneu) would be required to express, "Christ was not present with you" [Tittmann].<div eID="gen35485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">aliens--</hi>Greek, "alienated from," not merely "separated from." The Israelites were cut off from the commonwealth of God, but it was as being self-righteous, indolent, and unworthy, not as aliens and strangers [Chrysostom]. The expression, "alienated from," takes it for granted that the Gentiles, before they had apostatized from the primitive truth, had been sharers in light and life (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Ep 4:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.23">23</reference>). The hope of redemption through the Messiah, on their subsequent apostasy, was embodied into a definite "commonwealth" or polity, namely, that "of Israel," from which the Gentiles were alienated. Contrast <reference osisRef="Eph.2.13">Ep 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.6">Ep 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.4">4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.5">5</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Ps.147.20">Psa 147:20</reference>.<div eID="gen35486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35487" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covenants of promise--</hi>rather, "... of the promise," namely, "to thee and thy seed will I give this land" (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Ro 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.16">Ga 3:16</reference>). The plural implies the several renewals of the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and with the whole people at Sinai [Alford]. "The promise" is singular, to signify that the covenant, in reality, and substantially, is one and the same at all times, but only different in its accidents and external circumstances (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.1.1">He 1:1</reference>, "at sundry times and in divers manners").<div eID="gen35487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35488" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having no ... hope--</hi>beyond this life (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.19">1Co 15:19</reference>). The CONJECTURES of heathen philosophers as to a future life were at best vague and utterly unsatisfactory. They had no divine "promise," and therefore no sure ground of "hope." Epicurus and Aristotle did not believe in it at all. The Platonists believed the soul passed through perpetual changes, now happy, and then again miserable; the Stoics, that it existed no longer than till the time of the general burning up of all things.<div eID="gen35488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35489" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without God--</hi>Greek, "atheists," that is, they had not "God" in the sense we use the word, the Eternal Being who made and governs all things (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.14.15">Ac 14:15</reference>, "Turn from these vanities unto the living God who made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things therein"), whereas the Jews had distinct ideas of God and immortality. Compare also <reference osisRef="Gal.4.8">Ga 4:8</reference>, "Ye knew not God ... ye did service unto them which are no gods" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.5">1Th 4:5</reference>). So also pantheists are atheists, for an impersonal God is NO God, and an ideal immortality no immortality [Tholuck].<div eID="gen35489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35490" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the world--</hi>in contrast to belonging to "the commonwealth of Israel." Having their portion and their all in this godless vain world (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Psa 17:14</reference>), from which Christ delivers His people (<reference osisRef="John.15.19">Joh 15:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.14">17:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.1.4">Ga 1:4</reference>). <div eID="gen35490" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c550970fcb546dbc0f04debe97377e440e26c90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17606"/><div sID="gen35491" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17606"/><hi type="bold">13. now--</hi>in contrast to "at that time" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.12">Ep 2:12</reference>).<div eID="gen35491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35492" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Christ Jesus--</hi>"Jesus" is here added, whereas the expression before (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.12">Ep 2:12</reference>) had been merely "Christ," to mark that they know Christ as the personal Saviour, "Jesus."<div eID="gen35492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35493" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sometimes--</hi>Greek, "aforetime."<div eID="gen35493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">far off--</hi>the Jewish description of the Gentiles. Far off from God and from the people of God (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.17">Ep 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.19">Is 57:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.39">Ac 2:39</reference>).<div eID="gen35494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35495" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are--</hi>Greek, "have been."<div eID="gen35495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35496" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by--</hi>Greek, "in." Thus "the blood of Christ" is made the seal of a covenant IN which their nearness to God consists. In <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference>, where the blood is more directly spoken of as the instrument, it is "through His blood" [Alford]. <div eID="gen35496" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1ff85099d3d57827f6f49ba7ae37bdd4e0e1158: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17607"/><div sID="gen35497" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17607"/><hi type="bold">14. he--</hi>Greek, "Himself" alone, pre-eminently, and none else. Emphatical.<div eID="gen35497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35498" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our peace--</hi>not merely "Peacemaker," but "Himself" the price of our (Jews' and Gentiles' alike) peace with God, and so the bond of union between "both" in God. He took both into Himself, and reconciled them, united, to God, by His assuming our nature and our penal and legal liabilities (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.15">Ep 2:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.5">Is 9:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.5">53:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.5">Mi 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>). His title, "Shiloh," means the same (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Ge 49:10</reference>).<div eID="gen35498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the middle wall of partition--</hi>Greek, "... of the partition" or "fence"; the middle wall which parted Jew and Gentile. There was a balustrade of stone which separated the court of the Gentiles from the holy place, which it was death for a Gentile to pass. But this, though incidentally alluded to, was but a symbol of the partition itself, namely, "the enmity" between "both" and God (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.15">Ep 2:15</reference>), the real cause of separation from God, and so the mediate cause of their separation from one another. Hence there was a twofold wall of partition, one the inner wall, severing the Jewish people from entrance to the holy part of the temple where the priests officiated, the other the outer wall, separating the Gentile proselytes from access to the court of the Jews (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.7">Eze 44:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.21.28">Ac 21:28</reference>). Thus this twofold wall represented the Sinaitic law, which both severed all men, even the Jews, from access to God (through sin, which is the violation of the law), and also separated the Gentiles from the Jews. As the term "wall" implies the strength of the partition, so "fence" implies that it was easily removed by God when the due time came. <div eID="gen35499" type="x-p"/>
entries.888f52a9f0e32faffebbca4ea8b2e7506430b0b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17608"/><div sID="gen35500" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17608"/>15. Rather, make "enmity" an apposition to "the middle wall of partition"; "Hath broken down the middle wall of partition (not merely as English Version, 'between us,' but also between all men and God), to wit, the enmity (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.7">Ro 8:7</reference>) by His flesh" (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.2.16">Ep 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.3">Ro 8:3</reference>).<div eID="gen35500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the law of commandments contained in--</hi>Greek, "the law of the commandments (consisting) in ordinances." This law was "the partition" or "fence," which embodied the expression of the "enmity" (the "wrath" of God against our sin, and our enmity to Him, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.3">Ep 2:3</reference>) (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.15">Ro 4:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.20">5:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.7.10">7:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.7">8:7</reference>). Christ has in, or by, His crucified flesh, abolished it, so far as its condemning and enmity-creating power is concerned (<reference osisRef="Col.2.14">Col 2:14</reference>), substituting for it the law of love, which is the everlasting spirit of the law, and which flows from the realization in the soul of His love in His death for us. Translate what follows, "that He might make the two (Jews and Gentiles) into one new man." Not that He might merely reconcile the two to each other, but incorporate the two, reconciled in Him to God, into one new man; the old man to which both belonged, the enemy of God, having been slain in His flesh on the cross. Observe, too, ONE new man; we are all in God's sight but one in Christ, as we are but one in Adam [Alford].<div eID="gen35501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">making peace--</hi>primarily between all and God, secondarily between Jews and Gentiles; He being "our peace." This "peace-making" precedes its publication (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.17">Ep 2:17</reference>). <div eID="gen35502" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb711399c9e782a11d86eaf05ab936f50e165137: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17609"/><div sID="gen35503" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17609"/>16. Translate, "might altogether reconcile them both in one body (the Church, <reference osisRef="Col.3.15">Col 3:15</reference>) unto God through His cross." The Greek for "reconcile" (apocatalaxe), found only here and in <reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>, expresses not only a return to favor with one (catallage), but so to lay aside enmity that complete amity follows; to pass from enmity to complete reconciliation [Tittmann].<div eID="gen35503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35504" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">slain the enmity--</hi>namely, that had been between man and God; and so that between Jew and Gentile which had resulted from it. By His being slain, He slew it (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>).<div eID="gen35504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35505" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thereby--</hi>Greek, "therein"; "in" or "by the cross," that is, His crucifixion (<reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col 2:15</reference>). <div eID="gen35505" type="x-p"/>
entries.942ddee2d62804c6c60cfb704bf13fabde015a2e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17610"/><div sID="gen35506" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17610"/>17. Translate, "He came and announced glad tidings of peace." "He came" of His own free love, and "announced peace" with His own mouth to the apostles (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.36">Lu 24:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.20.19">Joh 20:19</reference>, 21, 26); and by them to others, through His Spirit present in His Church (<reference osisRef="John.14.18">Joh 14:18</reference>). <reference osisRef="Acts.26.23">Ac 26:23</reference> is strictly parallel; after His resurrection "He showed light to the people ('them that were nigh') and to the Gentiles ('you that were afar off')," by His Spirit in His ministers (compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.19">1Pe 3:19</reference>).<div eID="gen35506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and to them--</hi>The oldest manuscripts insert "peace" again: "And peace to them." The repetition implies the joy with which both alike would dwell again and again upon the welcome word "peace." So <reference osisRef="Isa.57.19">Is 57:19</reference>. <div eID="gen35507" type="x-p"/>
entries.191137f4df6656a45927be7fb8cf6f1454ef2282: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17611"/><div sID="gen35508" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17611"/>18. Translate, "For it is through Him (<reference osisRef="John.14.6">Joh 14:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.19">He 10:19</reference>) that we have our access (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.12">Ep 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.2">Ro 5:2</reference>), both of us, in (that is, united in, that is, "by," <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.13">1Co 12:13</reference>, Greek) one Spirit to the Father," namely, as our common Father, reconciled to both alike; whence flows the removal of all separation between Jew and Gentile. The oneness of "the Spirit," through which we both have our access, is necessarily followed by oneness of the body, the Church (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.16">Ep 2:16</reference>). The distinctness of persons in the Divine Trinity appears in this verse. It is also fatal to the theory of sacerdotal priests in the Gospel through whom alone the people can approach God. All alike, people and ministers, can draw nigh to God through Christ, their ever living Priest. <div eID="gen35508" type="x-p"/>
entries.349314517dcc6f9546e7880550ab1983bd515b4c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17612"/><div sID="gen35509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17612"/><hi type="bold">19. Now, therefore--</hi>rather, "So then" [Alford].<div eID="gen35509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35510" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foreigners--</hi>rather, "sojourners"; opposed to "members of the household," as "strangers" is to "fellow citizens." <reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">20</reference>, "conversation," Greek, "citizenship."<div eID="gen35510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but--</hi>The oldest manuscripts add, "are."<div eID="gen35511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with the saints--</hi>"the commonwealth of (spiritual) Israel" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.12">Ep 2:12</reference>).<div eID="gen35512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35513" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of God--</hi>THE Father; as Jesus Christ appears in <reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Ep 2:20</reference>, and THE Spirit in <reference osisRef="Eph.2.22">Ep 2:22</reference>. <div eID="gen35513" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c239c2ac8894ae923cb5f8dc96e03f0fc36a632: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17613"/><div sID="gen35514" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17613"/>20. Translate as Greek, "Built up upon," &c. (participle; having been built up upon; omit, therefore, "and are"). Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11">1Co 3:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.12">12</reference>. The same image in <reference osisRef="Eph.3.18">Ep 3:18</reference>, recurs in his address to the Ephesian elders (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.32">Ac 20:32</reference>), and in his Epistle to Timothy at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">1Ti 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2Ti 2:19</reference>), naturally suggested by the splendid architecture of Diana's temple; the glory of the Christian temple is eternal and real, not mere idolatrous gaud. The image of a building is appropriate also to the Jew-Christians; as the temple at Jerusalem was the stronghold of Judaism; as Diana's temple, of paganism.<div eID="gen35514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35515" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foundation of the apostles, &c.--</hi>that is, upon their ministry and living example (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.16.18">Mt 16:18</reference>). Christ Himself, the only true Foundation, was the grand subject of their ministry, and spring of their life. As one with Him and His fellow workers, they, too, in a secondary sense, are called "foundations" (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.14">Re 21:14</reference>). The "prophets" are joined with them closely; for the expression is here not "foundations of the apostles and the prophets," but "foundations of the apostles and prophets." For the doctrine of both was essentially one (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.10">1Pe 1:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.10">Re 19:10</reference>). The apostles take the precedency (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.24">Lu 10:24</reference>). Thus he appropriately shows regard to the claims of the Jews and Gentiles: "the prophets" representing the old Jewish dispensation, "the apostles" the new. The "prophets" of the new also are included. Bengel and Alford refer the meaning solely to these (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.5">Ep 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.11">4:11</reference>). These passages imply, I think, that the New Testament prophets are not excluded; but the apostle's plain reference to <reference osisRef="Ps.118.22">Psa 118:22</reference>, "the head stone of the corner," proves that the Old Testament prophets are a prominent thought. David is called a "prophet" in <reference osisRef="Acts.2.30">Ac 2:30</reference>. Compare also <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Is 28:16</reference>; another prophet present to the mind of Paul, which prophecy leans on the earlier one of Jacob (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.24">Ge 49:24</reference>). The sense of the context, too, suits this: Ye were once aliens from the commonwealth of Israel (in the time of her Old Testament prophets), but now ye are members of the true Israel, built upon the foundation of her New Testament apostles and Old Testament prophets. Paul continually identifies his teaching with that of Israel's old prophets (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.22">Ac 26:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.28.23">28:23</reference>). The costly foundation-stones of the temple (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.17">1Ki 5:17</reference>) typified the same truth (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.26">Jr 51:26</reference>). The same stone is at once the corner-stone and the foundation-stone on which the whole building rests. Paul supposes a stone or rock so large and so fashioned as to be both at once; supporting the whole as the foundation, and in part rising up at the extremities, so as to admit of the side walls meeting in it, and being united in it as the corner-stone [Zanchius]. As the corner-stone, it is conspicuous, as was Christ (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.6">1Pe 2:6</reference>), and coming in men's way may be stumbled over, as the Jews did at Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.42">Mt 21:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.7">1Pe 2:7</reference>). <div eID="gen35515" type="x-p"/>
entries.44294991ce782b5d933c0b8dd4228b7c0f7d03c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17614"/><div sID="gen35516" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17614"/><hi type="bold">21. In whom--</hi>as holding together the whole.<div eID="gen35516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35517" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fitly framed--</hi>so as exactly to fit together.<div eID="gen35517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35518" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">groweth--</hi>"is growing" continually. Here an additional thought is added to the image; the Church has the growth of a living organism, not the mere increase of a building. Compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1Pe 2:5</reference>; "lively stones ... built up a spiritual house." Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.4.16">Ep 4:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.6.12">Zec 6:12</reference>, "The Branch shall build the temple of the Lord," where similarly the growth of a branch, and the building of a temple, are joined.<div eID="gen35518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35519" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holy--</hi>as being the "habitation of God" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.22">Ep 2:22</reference>). So "in the Lord" (Christ) answers to "through the Spirit" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.22">Ep 2:22</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Eph.3.16">Ep 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.17">17</reference>). "Christ is the inclusive Head of all the building, the element in which it has its being and now its growth" [Alford]. <div eID="gen35519" type="x-p"/>
entries.f60bd9f4c26e9ed0461de2a40fbb7926732b8bd0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17615"/><div sID="gen35520" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17615"/><hi type="bold">22. are builded together--</hi>Translate, "are being builded together."<div eID="gen35520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35521" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through--</hi>Greek, "in the Spirit." God, by His Spirit in believers, has them for His habitation (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.16">1Co 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.19">6:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.16">2Co 6:16</reference>). <chapter eID="Eph.2"/>

entries.cb027b9610d57ebdd4f3c9e9135f47c81278da01: <div eID="gen50006" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen50007" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen50008" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen50008" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen50007" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen50009" type="x-p"/> The character of the Ephesians previously to their conversion to Christianity, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.1-Eph.2.3">Eph 2:1-3</reference>. By what virtue they were changed, and for what purpose, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.4-Eph.2.7">Eph 2:4-7</reference>. They were saved by faith, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.8">Eph 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.9">Eph 2:9</reference>. And created unto good works, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.10">Eph 2:10</reference>. The apostle enters into the particulars of their former miserable state, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.11">Eph 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.12">Eph 2:12</reference>. And those of their present happy state, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.13">Eph 2:13</reference>. Christ has broken down the middle wall of partition between the Jews and Gentiles, and proclaims reconciliation to both, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14-Eph.2.17">Eph 2:14-17</reference>. The glorious privileges of genuine believers, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.18-Eph.2.22">Eph 2:18-22</reference>. <div eID="gen50009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50010" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen50010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50011" type="x-p"/> And you hath he quickened - This chapter should not have been separated from the preceding, with which it is most intimately connected. As Christ fills the whole body of Christian believers with his fullness, (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.23">Eph 1:23</reference>), so had he dealt with the converted Ephesians, who before were dead in trespasses, and dead in sins. Death is often used by all writers, and in all nations, to express a state of extreme misery. The Ephesians, by trespassing and sinning, had brought themselves into a state of deplorable wretchedness, as had all the heathen nations; and having thus sinned against God, they were condemned by him, and might be considered as dead in law - incapable of performing any legal act, and always liable to the punishment of death, which they had deserved, and which was ready to be inflicted upon them. <div eID="gen50011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50012" type="x-p"/> Trespasses, παραπτωμασι, may signify the slightest deviation from the line and rule of moral equity, as well as any flagrant offense; for these are equally transgressions, as long as the sacred line that separates between vice and virtue is passed over. <div eID="gen50012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50013" type="x-p"/> Sins, ἁμαρτιαις, may probably mean here habitual transgression; sinning knowingly and daringly.
entries.f59228999c471a487d45e3e85b4284d02eebdd1f: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen50013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50014" type="x-p"/> Wherein in time past ye walked - There is much force in these expressions; the Ephesians had not sinned casually, or now and then, but continually; it was their continual employment; they walked in trespasses and sins: and this was not a solitary case, all the nations of the earth acted in the same way; it was the course of this world, κατα τον αιωνα του κοσμου τουτου, according to the life, mode of living, or successive ages of this world. The word αιων, the literal meaning of which is constant duration, is often applied to things which have a complete course, as the Jewish dispensation, a particular government, and the term of human life; so, here, the whole of life is a tissue of sin, from the cradle to the grave; every human soul, unsaved by Jesus Christ, continues to transgress. And the nominally Christian world is in the same state to the present day.
